channel.title: Philippine Trade News, Russia–Philippines Trade Link
channel.description: Short notes on Philippine imports, tariffs, prices and demand, with a link to the original publication. Collected twice a week.

item.title: Issue of 22 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The pork file is the one to watch: Manila is weighing a pause on import clearances, running a safeguard investigation and reviewing tariffs, while quota applications for next year are already open. Suppliers should first confirm with their Philippine buyer that a clearance is already issued before booking any shipment. The other items are scattered and the port congestion order is not in force yet, so build extra lead time into delivery plans and follow the tariff decisions expected in late October.

item.title: Issue of 19 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The items in this digest are scattered, but on pork they point the same way: duties are set to rise while existing stocks will already hold back buying for the coming months and into next year. Pork suppliers should confirm the rate and the timing with local importers before committing shipments. For perishables, the more relevant move is to check which partners will get the new cold storage capacity and on what terms they accept cargo. Rice purchases are rising on weather risk and mostly concern Asian suppliers, while the overall backdrop is that food prices remain the main concern for buyers, so price is the first thing an importer will ask about.

item.title: Issue of 12 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The main point here is the joint Russian-Philippine trade commission meeting in Manila in late November, where fertilizers, meat, grains, LNG, pharmaceuticals and equipment were named as priority areas. The rest of the news is scattered and mostly about Philippine agriculture, inflation and logistics. Pork exporters should check the tariff regime in advance since industry groups are pushing for higher duties, and the weak sugar crop, food inflation and possible port disruption in Manila matter for delivery timing and cost.

item.title: Issue of 8 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The items are a mixed bag, but the key point for Russian suppliers is that agricultural and energy trade with the Philippines is already moving, with pork and oil shipments back on track. Weak consumer spending and high inflation mean buyers will favour staples and feed ingredients over premium goods, and the proposed corn import quota plus another likely rice import record point the same way. In the coming weeks, confirm who the importer of record is (BOC accreditation) and how VAT is handled if you sell without a local company.

item.title: Issue of 5 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. El Nino is pushing the Philippines to import more food and fuel while rice prices and shipping capacity tighten, so demand for food and fuel cargo should hold. For Russian sellers that means deals are workable, but freight and port costs must be checked first, especially the disputed tariff increase in Cebu. The rest of the news on pork, poultry and electronics exports says little directly about Russia, though the Cebu fertilizer purchase shows where agricultural spending is going.

item.title: Issue of 1 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The items are a mixed bag: steel, poultry and pork rules, rice and corn supply, inflation and infrastructure. The one that matters most is food, since the Philippines will keep buying rice and corn abroad while costly transport and a weak peso squeeze importers, so check whether the corn import quota is widened and who already holds those volumes, as Argentina is pushing in. Steel runs the other way, with a long-term plan to cut import reliance, so the better angle is equipment and services for new mills, storage and the metro rather than finished steel. Also track the reclassification of pork cheeks and updates on poultry bans, since those decisions can change duties and market access with little notice.

item.title: Issue of 28 September 2026
item.description:
What this means. The news is mixed: pork imports are being tightened, while demand for poultry and rice is rising, and there are separate signals on rehabilitation equipment and agri-drones. The key point for Russian suppliers is pork, where quotas and higher tariffs are under discussion, so check the current tariff regime, permits, and frozen meat inspection rules before shipping. For poultry, demand is steady but competition and local output are growing, so prepare documents and pricing with logistics in mind, and watch customs enforcement changes and BAI ASF consultations because they affect delays and market access.
